title: Built-in Validation Attributes
description: Apply common validation rules to your models using built-in data annotation attributes.

blocks.text: Data annotations are attributes you place directly on model properties. They declare validation rules as part of the model definition rather than scattering checks throughout your controller code. This keeps validation logic close to the data it protects.

When model binding completes, ASP.NET Core automatically validates any model that has data annotations. It checks each attribute and records any failures in ModelState. If ModelState is not valid, the framework skips your action logic and returns errors to the client.

blocks.title: Server-Side First
blocks.text: Data annotations always run on the server. Client-side validation is an optional enhancement built on top of the same rules. Never rely on client-side validation alone for security.

ASP.NET Core ships with a set of attributes in the System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations namespace. Each attribute targets a specific type of rule. You can stack multiple attributes on the same property.

blocks.title: Built-in Attributes
items: [Required] - Ensures the value is not null or empty.
[StringLength(max)] - Limits the length of a string.
[MinLength(min)] - Ensures a string or collection meets a minimum length.
[Range(min, max)] - Checks that a numeric value falls within a range.
[EmailAddress] - Validates that a string is in email format.
[RegularExpression(pattern)] - Validates a string against a regex pattern.
[Compare(otherProperty)] - Ensures two properties match, useful for password confirmation.

blocks.text: A typical model for a product registration page might require a name, enforce a price range, and validate an image URL. All of these rules can be expressed with built-in attributes.

blocks.title: Product Model with Validation Attributes
blocks.content: This model demonstrates several built-in validation attributes working together.

blocks.text: Notice that each attribute can include a custom ErrorMessage. If validation fails, that message is stored in ModelState and returned to the view so the user sees a friendly explanation.

Once validation has run, your view can display the errors using validation tag helpers. The span element with asp-validation-for renders an error message for a single property. The div with asp-validation-summary displays all errors at once.

blocks.title: Razor View with Validation Messages
blocks.content: Use tag helpers to show validation feedback to the user.

blocks.title: Tip: Use All vs ModelOnly
blocks.text: asp-validation-summary='All' shows property errors plus model-level errors. Use 'ModelOnly' if you want to hide field-level messages and show only summary-level validation failures.

Validation runs after model binding finishes. The framework first checks that required values are present, then applies range and format rules. If a property fails [Required], other attributes on the same property are skipped for that property. This avoids confusing cascading errors.

terms.definition: An attribute applied to a model property or class that declares validation rules or display metadata.
A dictionary that tracks the validity of bound model data, including field-level and model-level errors.
A class derived from ValidationAttribute that enforces a specific rule, such as range or required.
A custom message shown to the user when a validation attribute fails.
A server-side component that enhances HTML elements with validation rendering, link generation, or other behavior.

blocks.title: Exercise: Validate an Event Registration Form
blocks.description: Build a model with multiple validation attributes and display errors in a Razor view.
steps: Create an EventRegistrationViewModel with properties: FullName, Email, Age, EventDate, and SessionCount.
Apply [Required], [EmailAddress], and [Phone] to Email and Phone.
Apply [DataType(DataType.Date)] and a [CustomValidation] or future date check to EventDate.
Build a Razor view with validation messages and test with valid and invalid inputs.
blocks.expectedOutcome: ModelState will be valid only when every rule passes. The view will display field-level error messages for each failed rule.

items.text: I know where validation runs in the request pipeline.
items.hint: After model binding and before the action body executes.

blocks.title: Summary
points: Data annotations attach validation rules directly to model properties.
Validation runs automatically after model binding.
Built-in attributes cover the most common rules: required, length, range, email, and URL.
Custom ErrorMessage strings make failures user-friendly.
asp-validation-for and asp-validation-summary render errors in the view.
blocks.takeaway: Data annotations give you a declarative, maintainable way to enforce rules at the model layer without writing repetitive controller code.
